AI Landing Zones

Three teams. One reusable foundation.What should every AI workload inherit?
Reusable guardrailsIdentityConnectivityGovernanceOperations
Scenario details

An AI landing zone is a repeatable foundation for deploying and operating AI workloads with enterprise identity, connectivity, governance and operational controls.

Today we’ll identify what is shared, what each workload owns, and the decisions needed to onboard our first AI workload.

The story is the AI landing zone: a foundation that teams can reuse without losing workload accountability. An internal assistant built with Microsoft Foundry is our example workload, not the subject of a separate application demo. Users enter through Teams, Microsoft 365 or web via configured integrations. Microsoft Copilot Studio remains an alternative UX or integration option.

Architecture details

The Agent Landing Zone and AI Gateway Landing Zone can be deployed together or independently. The accelerator is in preview; each Azure service has its own availability status. The connectivity hub and APIM are different responsibilities. Cloud channels do not require this connectivity hub. DNS is not an inline hop; firewall inspection depends on routing. The outline is not a single VNet.

Copilot Studio is SaaS, not deployed inside the illustrated VNet. It is an optional UX or integration choice, not the primary request path shown here. Channel integration and backend reachability are configured separately.

The documented Copilot Studio–Foundry agent connection is preview. It supports agents created in the new Foundry portal and requires the Foundry agent’s Activity protocol endpoint to be enabled. That endpoint is not enabled by default and currently requires REST API or Python SDK configuration; it cannot be enabled in the Foundry portal. The default Responses and A2A endpoints alone are insufficient.

Validate supported agent experience, endpoint configuration, identity, data handling and network reachability; neither platform automatically grants the other access.

Hub & Spoke Architecture · Private-hybrid example

One private-hybrid pattern, not a required path for cloud channels.

Connectivity details

This example shows an on-premises client calling APIM through private-hybrid connectivity. Cloud channels use their configured integration paths. The model and data paths are logical; supported networking depends on service configuration.

Clients / On-Premises

  • Enterprise apps and users reach Azure through the established hybrid network path — typically ExpressRoute or VPN into the hub VNet.
  • ExpressRoute private peering provides private hybrid connectivity; a VPN uses an encrypted tunnel over the internet. Private service access also needs supported endpoint configuration, DNS, routing, and authorization.
  • This is the enterprise perimeter — it stays customer-owned regardless of which VNet isolation model Foundry uses.

Connectivity hub — shared network services

  • ExpressRoute or VPN terminates at the hybrid gateway; hub routing provides reachability to connected application and shared-services networks.
  • Shared DNS, often using Azure DNS Private Resolver with private DNS zones, resolves private service names for Azure and on-premises callers. DNS is not an inline request hop.
  • Azure Firewall or an NVA inspects traffic only when the effective routes and supported network policies steer traffic through it.
  • APIM governs API requests. It is separate from the network hub and can be deployed in a shared-services spoke with supported private connectivity.

AI Gateway Landing Zone - hub for models

  • A logical API gateway hub, not the connectivity hub VNet. Placement may be in a separate shared-services spoke; verify inbound and outbound network support for the selected APIM tier.
  • Applies configured access control, token governance, routing and diagnostics to requests routed through this gateway.
  • Publishes API contracts — a single, governed front door for AI apps and agents.
  • Can be one deployment covering prod + non-prod, or split, depending on governance needs.
  • Supports configured token limits, routing and eligible caching; safely partition cached responses by authorization and workload context.

Agent Landing Zone - spoke for agents

  • Example isolation boundary: business unit or workload, based on governance, ownership, capacity and lifecycle requirements.
  • Isolation for model deployments, quotas, cost tracking, and operational ownership.
  • Templated and repeatable — new spokes onboard through infrastructure-as-code, not portal clicks.

Workload Data + Dependencies

  • Storage Account and Key Vault — included in this reference architecture; validate requirements for the selected hosting mode.
  • AI Search — customer-owned vector stores, required for the documented standard setup illustrated here.
  • Cosmos DB — conversation and agent state, required for this documented standard setup.
  • Private endpoints, private DNS, access permissions, and public-network restrictions must be configured together.

AI Landing Zone Blueprint

Govern once, delegate deliberately

  • Management groups organize subscriptions and inherited policy assignments. Microsoft Entra ID supplies identities; role assignments define access at the appropriate scope.
  • Policy, identity permissions, and network controls solve different problems. None substitutes for the others.

Connectivity is a shared platform capability

  • Hybrid connectivity, DNS resolution, routing, and egress controls establish approved network paths into and out of workload environments.
  • Private endpoints require working DNS and routing, supported service configuration, and appropriate public-access restrictions. Peering alone does not provide end-to-end private access.

A governed model access point

  • Applications call an APIM API, which can apply identity checks, consumer limits, backend selection, and diagnostics before forwarding a model request.
  • The gateway is a logical shared service. Its subscription and network placement depend on the APIM tier and enterprise topology; it need not reside inside the connectivity hub.
  • The arrows show a conceptual application-to-gateway-to-model request. They do not imply that every tool call or retrieval operation passes through APIM.

The application owns the user-facing workflow

  • The conversational UX can be a custom app or Copilot Studio. Copilot Studio runs outside the Azure landing zone and connects through supported integrations; the box here represents Azure-side backend orchestration.
  • Application orchestration assembles prompts, retrieves authorized context, and controls which tools or actions may run.
  • Document permissions and approval for high-impact actions belong in the application design, not merely in a network diagram.

A repeatable environment for AI workloads

  • Foundry projects organize AI development and access to model and agent capabilities. The workload team owns evaluations, releases, and operational readiness.
  • Separate subscriptions, resources, projects, or environments according to the required isolation boundary. A project is not automatically a separate network or subscription boundary.

Dependencies follow the use case

  • A model-only application may need no search index. Retrieval adds governed data access; stateful agents and tools introduce their own runtime and storage requirements.
  • Search, storage, state stores, and secrets services are examples, not a mandatory bundle. Both applications and agent runtimes may access these dependencies.

Operate the platform and workload together

  • Correlate gateway, application, and model diagnostics while protecting prompt and response data. Define retention, access, and incident ownership.
  • Use infrastructure as code for repeatable environments. Assign budgets and cost ownership; budget alerts alone do not stop spending.

Microsoft-Managed vs. Customer-Managed VNet

Same VNet, different subnets. The delegated subnet supplies runtime IPs for hosted Micro VMs and project data proxies. The separate, nondelegated subnet holds private endpoint NICs; the managed data services themselves are not deployed into that subnet. This example places both subnets in one VNet; private endpoints can also be reached in a peered VNet with the appropriate routing and DNS.

Firewall placement is separate. If Azure Firewall is used, it lives in its own dedicated AzureFirewallSubnet, often in the connectivity hub. UDRs and network rules control supported outbound paths; private endpoint traffic is not automatically routed through the firewall.

Microsoft-Managed VNet

  • Microsoft handles subnet range, IP selection, and delegation inside the managed network.
  • Managed private endpoints can provide private access to supported, configured dependencies, with required permissions and approvals.
  • No customer-owned firewall or UDR design inside the managed VNet. Optional FQDN outbound rules use a Microsoft-managed Azure Firewall and can incur charges.
  • Trade-off: customer-controlled routing and inspection are constrained. Validate connectivity and diagnostics support for the selected service and deployment mode.

Customer-Managed VNet (BYO)

  • Customer-controlled Azure Firewall/NVA integration, user-defined routes and peering, subject to the selected runtime's supported paths.
  • Connects to hub/spoke, shared services, or on-premises via ExpressRoute/VPN.
  • Separate subnets: delegate the agent runtime subnet to Microsoft.App/environments; place private endpoint NICs in a different, nondelegated subnet.
  • Encryption key ownership is a separate service-level decision, not a property of a private endpoint.
  • Trade-off: subnet delegation and deployment-path-specific capability configuration. /27 is the documented minimum for the relevant agent subnet, not a production recommendation. Start production sizing at /24 or larger and validate peak use; these sizes do not describe Microsoft-managed subnet control.
Network design decision: private connectivity alone does not require a customer-managed runtime VNet. Evaluate BYO when you need customer-controlled routing, inspection, or integration with existing networks. Confirm supported inbound and outbound paths for the selected Foundry service and deployment mode. The enterprise perimeter remains a separate responsibility.

AI Landing Zones in Detail

Apps & Agents (Consumers)

  • A shared enforcement point for requests routed through the gateway, with backend identity and network controls configured to prevent unintended bypass.
  • Consumers are identified by subscription key or Entra identity, never by a shared secret baked into code.

APIM Gateway

  • Applies configured access control, token governance, routing and diagnostics to requests routed through this gateway.
  • Publishes API contracts — a single, governed front door for AI apps and agents.
  • Can be one deployment covering prod + non-prod, or split, depending on governance needs.
  • Supports configured token limits, routing and eligible caching; safely partition cached responses by authorization and workload context.

Foundry Spokes

  • Example isolation boundary: business unit or workload, based on governance, ownership, capacity and lifecycle requirements.
  • New spokes plug into the same gateway contract without renegotiating access for every consumer.

Shared Services

  • Choose workspace boundaries based on access, residency, retention and operating requirements. Cross-workspace queries are supported.
  • Key Vault can hold gateway certificates and secrets. Configure Entra identity validation and least-privilege backend access for this identity-first example.

Management Group (AI subscriptions)

Policy assigned once here is inherited by every subscription and resource underneath — this is what makes the next four controls consistent across the whole estate instead of configured per-subscription.

Policy recommendations: names, effects, scopes, owners and exceptions

Foundry projects and model deployments are resource relationships, not replacements for Azure scope levels. Prefer Entra identities and least-privilege RBAC; disable local key authentication where supported. Managed identities are not covered by workload-identity Conditional Access.

Workspace design recommendation: choose workspace boundaries based on access, residency, retention and operating requirements. Cross-workspace queries are supported.

Networking Deep Dive

Foundry Agent Service networking: request paths, shared subnet capacity, outbound controls, and operational checks.

BYO VNet: trace an agent request

Client and application owner

Clients need both network reachability and a valid identity. An APIM gateway can govern client requests, but it is not the agent runtime's outbound firewall.

Inbound access is a separate decision

Requests enter the Foundry endpoint over HTTPS 443. Configure private inbound connectivity and DNS for clients when required; attaching a delegated subnet for outbound traffic does not make inbound access private automatically.

Hosted agent: your code, managed runtime

You control the container image, agent code, and supported CPU/memory configuration, not the underlying Micro VM operating system. Hosted sessions consume delegated-subnet IP capacity. Direct outbound calls made by agent code can use the Micro VM's NIC; registered tool calls use the data proxy path.

Shared execution service

Both agent types use the platform Tools Service. Prompt agents run on Microsoft-managed compute without a customer Micro VM on this path. Tool authorization and least-privilege resource permissions remain necessary.

Project-level private egress

Each project has a dedicated, single-tenant data proxy. Its infrastructure consumes delegated-subnet IPs and can scale with traffic. Microsoft operates this component; the customer configures network boundaries and permitted destinations, not its containers or host OS.

Private endpoints are not the service itself

Place private endpoints in a separate, nondelegated subnet and configure the matching DNS zones. Storage, databases, and Key Vault remain managed services behind those endpoints. Endpoint approval, DNS, routing, public-access settings, and data-plane permissions must all align.

Microsoft operates

The Foundry endpoint, Tools Service, runtime hosts, and project data proxies.

You configure

BYO address space, delegation, DNS, private endpoints, routes, network rules, and resource permissions.

Two outbound paths

Registered tool calls use the data proxy. Hosted agent code can also make direct calls through its runtime NIC.

Shared subnet capacity, not a per-agent allocation

The delegated subnet is configured at the Foundry account level and shared across its projects and agent types. Start production planning at /24 or larger, then size for actual peak usage and temporary maintenance capacity.

Usable subnet IPs

Address count minus the five addresses reserved by Azure.

Planning envelope

Combined IP use kept below 80%: hosted sessions plus project-level networking components.

IPs left outside the envelope

Headroom for scaling, rolling upgrades, and overlapping old/new infrastructure.

What consumes capacity?

Hosted sessions normally map 1:1 to usable IPs. Data proxies and other project-level networking components also consume addresses. Prompt agent versions do not consume their own runtime IPs, but their project networking still does.

Do not size from a fixed replica-to-IP formula. Real consumption depends on concurrency, project traffic, scale-out, and platform maintenance. Low-traffic project counts are not a guarantee of capacity under load.

Subnet capacity is not the session quota

All Foundry accounts and projects in the same subscription and region share the regional session quota. A larger subnet does not raise it. Check current regional limits and request an increase when necessary.

A support-approved mapping of up to 10 sessions per IP may be available, subject to regional capacity. Do not assume this mapping in the default address plan.

Address space and subnet prerequisites
  • Use non-overlapping RFC1918 space for this example. Confirm support for other ranges against the selected deployment path before allocation.
  • Current setup guidance permits specified CGNAT ranges while the networking deep dive excludes them. Confirm the applicable deployment path before allocation; do not treat either statement as universal.
  • Delegate the runtime subnet to Microsoft.App/environments; /27 is the documented minimum for the relevant path, not a production recommendation. Start production planning at /24 or larger.
  • Use a separate subnet for private endpoints. Check overlap across peered VNets and hybrid routes before allocation.

Microsoft-managed VNet: choose the outbound boundary

Microsoft manages the network, subnet sizing, and runtime IP allocation. You choose isolation settings, outbound rules, private connections, approvals, and resource permissions.

01 / Runtime

Managed agent network

Hosted and prompt agents use the account's managed outbound boundary.

02 / Control

03 / Destination

Approved outbound: firewall and cost implications

Approved outbound uses private endpoints, service tags, and optional FQDN rules. FQDN rules use a Microsoft-managed Azure Firewall and support ports 80 and 443; budget for the associated firewall charges.

You cannot insert your own Azure Firewall or NVA into this managed network, or share its managed firewall across Foundry accounts. This is different from routing BYO subnet traffic through your own firewall.

Private connections and on-premises access

Managed private endpoints are platform-managed; they do not create customer-visible NICs in your own VNet. Approve the target resource connections and configure the required identities.

For on-premises services, use a supported private connectivity pattern, such as a private endpoint to Application Gateway with an appropriately configured backend. Verify protocol and backend support; do not assume direct peering into the managed VNet.

Mode changes and migration constraints

These buttons only change this illustration. In Azure, enabled managed isolation cannot simply be disabled; approved-only outbound cannot be relaxed back to internet outbound. Moving from a custom VNet setup to managed networking requires redeployment.

Confirm current region, API, agent type, tool, and deployment-path support before choosing the operating model. Inbound private access is still configured separately.

Private connectivity requires a complete chain

01 / Resolve

DNS returns the private IP

Check the normal service hostname from the actual calling network, including on-premises clients.

02 / Reach

Routing and rules allow it

Confirm endpoint approval, peering or hybrid routes, NSGs, and the service's required ports.

03 / Authorize

The identity has access

Verify the calling identity and resource data-plane roles. A private IP does not grant permission.

Examples, not a complete zone list. Foundry, Search, Cosmos DB, and other Storage subresources require their own matching zones. Link the relevant VNets or provide resolution through a shared DNS design. On-premises DNS typically forwards through an Azure-side resolver.

Validate the service's normal hostname with nslookup from the calling network. Connect using that hostname, not a hardcoded private IP, so TLS hostname checks continue to work.

BYO egress, routes, and hybrid connectivity

Use supported UDR and firewall/NVA configurations to control outbound paths. Include required platform dependencies as well as approved workload destinations; a blanket deny without the necessary rules can prevent provisioning or execution.

Private endpoint traffic is not automatically inspected by your firewall. Effective routes and private endpoint network-policy settings determine the path. ExpressRoute or VPN provides connectivity, not DNS resolution or resource authorization.

Capacity symptoms and escalation
  • Data proxy 5xx: investigate proxy health and capacity; the status alone does not prove IP exhaustion.
  • Hosted session HTTP 429 subnet_exhausted: investigate available subnet capacity during session creation or resume.
  • New project provisioning failure: check address availability, deployment errors, capability configuration, and provisioning permissions.

Direct delegated-subnet utilization is not currently exposed in the portal. Monitor these service signals and record timestamps, affected projects, region, concurrency, and recent changes. For persistent exhaustion, plan additional capacity or a new Foundry instance with a fresh subnet; coordinate with support.

Timeouts, name resolution, and authorization errors
  • Name lookup fails or returns a public IP: check zone records, VNet links, and DNS forwarding.
  • Connection times out: inspect effective routes, endpoint approval, NSG/firewall decisions, ports, and service health.
  • 401 / 403: inspect token audience, identity, data-plane roles, and service access rules; not every 403 is a routing issue.
  • Provisioning succeeds but runtime fails: the provisioning caller and runtime project identity can require different permissions.
